opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when we started thinking about Genie 3, the starting point was really looking at what we'd learned from Genie 2 and from our work on video generation with Veo, and asking: what's actually missing for this to feel like a real, explorable world rather than a short, impressive clip?

A few things stood out. The first was real-time interactivity. With earlier versions, you could generate something that looked like a game environment, but there was latency, and it didn't feel like you were actually *in* it. So a big goal was getting to the point where you press a key and the world responds immediately, frame by frame, at a reasonable resolution and frame rate. That turned out to be a pretty hard technical problem, because the model has to generate each new frame autoregressively, taking into account everything that's happened before and the action the user just took, and it has to do that many times per second.

The second thing was consistency over time. If you walk away from something and then turn back around, it should still be there, and it should look the same. With earlier models, the world would kind of drift or forget itself after a few seconds. We wanted environments that stay coherent for minutes, not seconds. Interestingly, we don't build an explicit 3D representation to get that. It's something that emerges from the model learning to attend back over its own history, which I think is one of the more exciting results.

And the third piece was making the world more controllable and more open-ended. Not just "here's a scene, walk around it," but being able to describe a world with text, and then even change things while you're in it, like changing the weather or introducing new objects or characters. We call those promptable world events.

Underneath all of that is a bigger motivation. We see world models as a key step toward more general AI, because they give you a way to train and evaluate agents in rich, diverse environments that you could never hand-build. So taking Genie to the next level wasn't only about making cooler demos. It was about building something that could actually serve as a training ground for embodied agents, and also open up new creative and educational experiences along the way.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that when we finished Genie 3, we were kind of amazed by it ourselves, but we also had a pretty clear list of things that bothered us. Genie 3 was really the first time we had a world model that you could interact with in real time, at 24 frames per second, and that would stay consistent for a few minutes. That was a huge step from Genie 2, where you had maybe ten or twenty seconds before things started to drift. But a few minutes is still a few minutes. And the question we kept asking was: what does it mean for a world to actually feel like a world, and not like a very good video that happens to respond to your input?

So we ended up thinking about it along a few axes. The first one is consistency and memory. If you walk away from something and come back, is it still there? In Genie 3 we got that working to a degree, and it emerged from training rather than from us building an explicit 3D representation, which was surprising and exciting. But we wanted to push it much further, both in duration and in how robust it is to the kinds of things people actually do, which is turn around, go through doors, revisit places.

The second axis is the richness of the interaction. Navigation is a fairly narrow kind of interaction. You press forward, you look around. Real environments have objects that you pick up, that break, that affect each other. We introduced what we called promptable world events in Genie 3, where you could text-prompt a change into the world mid-stream, and that was a glimpse of something more general. The next step is making the world respond to a much wider range of actions in a way that's physically plausible, and having the model understand causality rather than just appearance.

And the third axis, which is maybe the one I care most about, is what the thing is for. It's a lot of fun to generate a world and walk around in it, but the reason we build these at DeepMind is that we think world models are a path toward more general agents. An agent needs somewhere to practice, and it needs an unlimited supply of situations it hasn't seen before. So a lot of our thinking about the next level has been about making the worlds useful as training environments. That means being able to specify them precisely, being able to run them long enough for an agent to pursue a goal, and having the dynamics be faithful enough that what the agent learns transfers.

So it's less about one big leap and more about closing the gap between "impressive demo" and something you'd actually trust as a simulator. And honestly, each of those axes turned out to be its own research problem.

astra-6.text:
For me, the question was: how do we move from generating something that looks like a world to something you can actually interact with? Once a user is in control, they can do things you didn’t anticipate. The model has to respond to those actions while keeping the world coherent.

So I think about the next level in terms of that experience. Can you explore for longer? Can you turn away from something and come back to a place that still makes sense? Do your actions have consequences that persist? Visual quality matters, but it’s that combination of responsiveness and consistency that makes it feel like a world rather than a video.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the next level was about making the world feel more consistent and responsive. It’s one thing to generate a compelling moment; it’s another to let someone interact with an environment and have it continue to make sense as they move around and make choices.

So we thought about it as a combination of capabilities: visual quality, real-time interaction, and memory of what has happened. If you turn away from something and then come back, you want to feel that you’re returning to the same place. And your actions should have consequences that persist.

That changes the challenge from generating a sequence of images to maintaining a world. The question becomes: how do we give the user more freedom while keeping that world coherent?
